parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what is random for a single unstable nucleus - it is not when it will decay, but the chance it decays in the next second.
Hint 2: A good definition needs both ideas of probability and per unit time, not just a fraction or a rate of the whole sample.
parts.proper_answer: The probability of decay of a nucleus per unit time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What lambda really means**
Think of one single iodine nucleus sitting there. You cannot say when it will decay because decay is spontaneous and random. What you can say is how likely it is to decay in the next second. That likelihood is $\lambda$.

Step 2: **Building the precise definition**
So $\lambda$ is not the number of decays per second, that is activity $A$. It is the probability per unit time. In symbols: $$ A = \lambda N $$ where $N$ is the number of undecayed nuclei present. A complete 2-mark definition is: probability that a nucleus will decay per unit time.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A sample of radioactive iodine-131 ($^{131}_{53}\text{I}$) of mass $5.87 \times 10^{-10} \text{kg}$ has an activity of $2.92 \times 10^{9} \text{Bq}$.

Determine the decay constant of iodine-131.
hints: Hint 1: You are given the total mass of the sample and the total activity, but the decay law links activity to the number of nuclei $N$, not directly to mass. How can you turn kg into a count of atoms?
Hint 2: Recall that activity and number of nuclei are linked by $A = \lambda N$, so you will need $N$ first using $N = m / m_{atom}$ and $m_{atom} = 131u$.
Hint 3: Remember $1u = 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$, calculate $N$ to about 3 s.f., then rearrange to $\lambda = A/N$ and check the unit $\text{s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the mass of one iodine-131 nucleus**
The nucleon number is 131, so one atom has mass about $131$ atomic mass units. With $1u = 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$: $$ m_{atom} = 131 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg} $$ $$ m_{atom} \approx 2.17 \times 10^{-25} \text{ kg} $$ This is tiny, which is why even $10^{-10} \text{ kg}$ contains trillions of atoms.

Step 2: **Find how many nuclei are in the sample**
Divide total mass by mass per atom: $$ N = \frac{m}{m_{atom}} = \frac{5.87 \times 10^{-10}}{2.17 \times 10^{-25}} $$ $$ N \approx 2.70 \times 10^{15} $$ No unit - it is just a number of nuclei.

Step 3: **Use activity to get the decay constant**
Activity is the total decay rate: $$ A = \lambda N $$ Rearrange before putting numbers in: $$ \lambda = \frac{A}{N} = \frac{2.92 \times 10^{9}}{2.70 \times 10^{15}} $$ $$ \lambda \approx 1.08 \times 10^{-6} \text{ s}^{-1} $$ That small value tells you iodine-131 decays slowly on a per-second, per-nucleus basis, even though the huge $N$ gives a large activity.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why a detector placed near to the sample in (b) would record a count rate much less than $2.92 \times 10^{9}$ counts per second.
hints: Hint 1: Picture the radiation leaving the sample in all directions in space - does all of it head toward the small window of the detector?
Hint 2: Think about what happens to the radiation on its way to the detector, and whether a real detector counts every particle that enters it.
parts.proper_answer: 1. Radiation is emitted isotropically in all directions, so only a small fraction enters the detector window. 2. Some radiation is absorbed in the air / sample / detector casing, and the detector has less than 100% efficiency / dead time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Geometry - most radiation misses the detector**
Activity $2.92 \times 10^{9} \text{ Bq}$ means that many decays per second in all directions. A detector placed nearby only subtends a small solid angle at the source. Most alpha, beta and gamma photons fly off away from the detector and are never counted.

Step 2: **Loss and efficiency - not everything arriving is counted**
Even the radiation heading toward the detector can be absorbed in the sample itself, in the air between source and detector, or in the detector window. Also no detector is perfect - some particles pass through without causing a count, and at very high rates the detector has dead time while processing one pulse. So measured count rate $<<$ true activity.
